metadata.title: Developments in Formal Proofs

extraction_notes.note: Four-Color, Prime Number, Brouwer and central limit theorems are stated only as proof-assistant code listings (lstlisting); the listing text is taken verbatim as the statement. The Coq/HOL listings restating the Odd Order theorem and the Kepler conjecture got no node (repeated statements), and the HoTT BG-connected lemma listing stays inside example ExP4.
theorem or remark: the formal verification of the HOL Light kernel in HOL (a model of HOL inside HOL with a large cardinal) is a cited result reported in prose, kept as an external theorem.
definition or assumption: the ten HOL inference rules are stipulations of the logic, typed as definitions (one per rule).
Prose outlines of other authors' proofs (Odd Order theorem, Peterfalvi's character-matrix case analysis) are emitted as external proof nodes; their extent and the proved result are judgment.

Discursive material on ML/OCaml, CakeML, verified compilers, the MESON procedure, automation success rates, Bourbaki's objections and future work was left out as having no mathematical statement; the definitions of p-local, CN-group and Frobenius group sit inside proof outline PP2 as steps.

metadata.extraction_comment: A Bourbaki seminar survey; almost every node is a cited or standard result (origin external), with the HOL consistency proof sketch the main argued content.

nodes.name: proof assistant
nodes.statement: A proof assistant is interactive computer software that humans use to prepare scripts of mathematical proofs.
differentia: that humans use to prepare scripts of mathematical proofs

nodes.name: formal proof
nodes.statement: A {\it formal proof} is one that has been verified from first principles (generally by computer).
differentia: verified from first principles (generally by computer)

nodes.name: simple type system
nodes.statement: Naively, a simple type system is a countable collection of disjoint nonempty sets called types.
nodes.genus: countable collection of disjoint nonempty sets

nodes.name: function type $A\to B$
nodes.statement: The collection of types satisfies a closure property: for every two types $A$ and $B$, there is a further type, denoted $A\to B$, that can be identified with the set of functions from $A$ to $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Types are closed under forming the function type $A\to B$, identified with functions from $A$ to $B$.

nodes.name: terms
nodes.statement: In addition to types, there are terms, which are thought of as elements of types. Each term $t$ has a unique type $A$.

nodes.name: typing judgement $t:A$
nodes.statement: This relationship between a term and its type is denoted $t:A$. In particular, $f:A\to B$ denotes a term $f$ of type $A\to B$.

nodes.name: type variables
nodes.statement: There are variables that range over types called {\it type variables}, and another collection of variables that run over terms.

nodes.name: set-theoretic interpretation $M$ of HOL types
nodes.statement: The interpretation of variable-free types as sets is recursively defined. We use a superscript $M$ to mark the interpretation of a type as a set. Specifically, the types in HOL are generated by the boolean type $\op{\tt bool}$ (which we interpret as a set $\op{\tt bool}^M=\{\downvdash ,\upvdash \}$ of cardinality two with labeled elements representing true and false) and the infinite type $I$ (which we interpret as a countably infinite set $I^M$). Recursively, for any two variable-free types $A$ and $B$, the type $A\to B$ is interpreted as the set $(A\to B)^M$ of all functions from $A^M$ to $B^M$. We can arrange that the sets interpreting these types are all disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Variable-free HOL types are interpreted recursively in ZFC: bool as a 2-element set, $I$ as a countably infinite set, $A\to B$ as all functions $A^M\to B^M$.

nodes.name: collection ${\mathcal T}$ of type interpretations
nodes.statement: In summary so far, we fix an interpretation $M$, determining a countable collection ${\mathcal T} =\{A^M\}$ of nonempty sets in ZFC.

nodes.name: valuation
nodes.statement: We now extend our interpretation $M$ to a {\it valuation} $v=(M,v_1,v_2)$, where $v_1$ is a function from the set of type variables in HOL to ${\mathcal T}$, and $v_2$ is a function from the set of term variables in HOL to $\bigcup{\mathcal T}$. The valuation $v$ extends recursively to give a mapping that assigns a set $A^{v}\in {\mathcal T}$ to every type $A$. We require $v_2$ to be chosen so that whenever $x$ is a variable of type $A$, then $x^{v_2} \in A^v$. The valuation $v$ extends recursively to give a mapping on all terms: \[ t\mapsto t^v \in A^v \in {\mathcal T}, \quad \text{for all } t:A. \]
nodes.statement_short: A valuation $v=(M,v_1,v_2)$ assigns sets in $\mathcal T$ to type variables and type-respecting elements to term variables, extending recursively to all types and terms.

nodes.name: interpretation of HOL equality
nodes.statement: For example, for every type $A$, there is a HOL term $(=)$ of type $A\to (A\to \op{\tt bool})$ representing equality for that type.\footnote{The convention in HOL is to curry functions: using the bijection $X^{Y \times Z} = (X^Z)^Y$ to write a function whose domain is a product as a function of a single argument taking values in a function space. In particular, equality is a curried function of type $A\to (A \to\op{\tt bool})$ rather than a relation on $A\times A$.} This term is interpreted as the function in $(A\to (A\to\op{\tt bool}))^v$ that maps $a\in A^{v}$ to the delta function $\delta_a$ supported at $a$ (where the support of the function means the preimage of $\downvdash$).
nodes.statement_short: The equality term of type $A\to(A\to bool)$ is interpreted as mapping $a$ to the delta function $\delta_a$.

nodes.name: sequent
nodes.statement: A {\it sequent} is a pair $(L,t)$, traditionally written $L\vdash t$, where $L$ is a finite set of terms called the {\it assumptions}, and $t$ is a term called the {\it conclusion}. The terms of $L$ and $t$ must all have type $\op{\tt bool}$. If $L$ is empty, it is omitted from the notation.
differentia: $L$ is a finite set of terms called the {\it assumptions}
$t$ is a term called the {\it conclusion}
The terms of $L$ and $t$ must all have type $\op{\tt bool}$.

nodes.name: logically valid sequent
nodes.statement: If $L$ is a finite set of boolean terms, and if $v$ is a valuation extending $M$, write $L^{v}$ for the corresponding set of elements of the set $\op{\tt bool}^M$. We say a sequent $L \vdash t$ is {\it logically valid} if for every valuation $v$ for which every element of $L^{v}$ is $\downvdash \in \op{\tt bool}^M$, we also have $t^{v}=\downvdash $ in $\op{\tt bool}^M$.
nodes.statement_short: A sequent is logically valid if every valuation making all assumptions true makes the conclusion true.

nodes.name: theorem in HOL
nodes.statement: A {\it theorem} in HOL is a sequent that is generated from the mathematical axioms and rules of logic.
differentia: generated from the mathematical axioms and rules of logic

nodes.name: Consistency of HOL relative to ZFC
nodes.statement: If ZFC is consistent, then HOL is consistent.
conclusions: HOL is consistent.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of consistency of HOL
nodes.statement: We give the proof in ZFC. Here, HOL is treated purely syntactically as a set of strings in a formal language. We run through the rules of logic of HOL one by one and check that each one preserves validity.\footnote{There are ten such rules, giving the behavior of equality, $\lambda$-abstractions, $\beta$-reduction, and the discharge of assumptions. For reference purposes, an appendix lists the inference rules of HOL. The analysis in this section omits the rules for the creation of new term constants and types.} For example, the reflexive law of equality in HOL states that for any term $t$ of any type $A$, we have a theorem $\vdash t = t$. By the interpretation of equality described above, under any valuation $v$, this equation is interpreted as the value $\delta_{t^{v}}(t^{v})\in\op{\tt bool}^M$, which is $\downvdash $. Hence the reflexive law preserves validity. The other rules (transitivity of equality, and so forth) are checked similarly. We may well-order each set in the collection ${\mathcal T}$. HOL posits a choice operator of type $(A\to\op{\tt bool})\to A$ for every type $A$. The well-ordering allows us to interpret HOL's choice operator as an operator that maps a function $f\in (A\to\op{\tt bool})^v$ with nonempty support to the minimal element of its support. We run through the mathematical axioms of HOL and check their validity. There are only three. The {\it axiom of infinity} positing the existence of an infinite type $I$ is logically valid by our requirement to interpret $I$ as a countably infinite set. The {\it axiom of choice} is logically valid by the well-ordering we have placed on the sets $A^M$. The {\it axiom of extensionality} also holds in this model, because it holds for sets. Thus, every axiom is logically valid. Since all axioms are logically valid and every rule of inference preserves validity, every theorem is logically valid. There is a boolean constant $\op{\tt FALSE}$ in HOL. It is defined to be the term $\forall p.~p$. An easy calculation based on its definition gives that $\op{\tt FALSE}^v = \upvdash$ for every valuation $v$. Hence, $\vdash \op{\tt FALSE}$ is not a logically valid sequent, and not a theorem. This proves HOL consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Build a set-theoretic model of HOL in ZFC: every rule preserves validity and every axiom is valid, while FALSE is interpreted as false, so FALSE is not a theorem.

nodes.name: HOL in HOL (formal verification of the HOL Light kernel)
nodes.statement: The correctness of the kernel has been formally verified, using the HOL Light proof assistant itself (extended by a large cardinal) \cite{HaSelf}.\footnote{A large cardinal axiom gives the existence of a large type corresponding to the set $\bigcup{\mathcal T}$ that we used above in the construction of a model. By G\"odel, we do not expect to construct a model of HOL in HOL except by adding an axiom to strengthen the system.} Specifically, a model of HOL can be built inside HOL itself along the same lines as the model of HOL in ZFC described above.
nodes.section: 1.4 Verification of the code that implements HOL Light
nodes.statement_short: The HOL Light kernel is verified correct in HOL Light extended by a large cardinal, by building a model of HOL inside HOL.
assumptions: using the HOL Light proof assistant itself (extended by a large cardinal)
conclusions: The correctness of the kernel has been formally verified
a model of HOL can be built inside HOL itself

nodes.name: Feit-Thompson Odd Order Theorem
nodes.statement: All finite groups of odd order are solvable.
nodes.section: 2 Advanced developments in Coq: The Odd Order theorem
conclusions: are solvable.

nodes.name: Outline of the proof of the Odd Order theorem
nodes.statement: In very brief terms, the proof starts by assuming a minimal counterexample to the statement. This counterexample will be a finite simple group $G$ of odd order in which every proper subgroup is solvable. Each maximal subgroup of $G$ is {\it $p$-local}; that is, the normalizer of a nontrivial subgroup of $G$ of $p$-power order, for some prime $p$. The first major part of the proof of the Odd Order theorem consists in establishing restrictions on the structure of the maximal subgroups and their embeddings into $G$. In the special case when $G$ is a {\it $CN$-group} (a group whose centralizers of non-identity elements are all nilpotent), the maximal subgroups are {\it Frobenius groups} \cite{FHT}. A Frobenius group is a nontrivial semidirect product $K\rtimes H$, where $H$ is disjoint from its conjugates, and $H$ is its own normalizer \cite[Th. 7.7]{gorenstein2007finite}. In the general case, the strategy is to prove that as many of the maximal subgroups as possible are as close as possible to being Frobenius groups. This strategy encounters many exceptions and detours, but eventually the local analysis shows that the maximal subgroups are mostly Frobenius-like \cite[Sec. 16]{bender1994local}. The second major portion of the proof uses the complex character theory of $G$ to obtain inequalities over the real numbers that restrict and ultimately eliminate all possibilities for $G$. The final part of the proof uses generators and relations to remove a special case in which there are maximal subgroups isomorphic to the group of all permutations of a finite field $\ring{F}$ of the form $x \mapsto a\, \sigma (x) + b$, where $\sigma$ is a field automorphism, $a,b\in\ring{F}$, and $a$ is an element of norm $1$. It is in this part of the proof that Galois theory is most relevant.
nodes.section: 2 Advanced developments in Coq: The Odd Order theorem
nodes.statement_short: Minimal counterexample: local analysis forces maximal subgroups to be nearly Frobenius, character theory then yields contradictory inequalities, and generators-and-relations remove a last special case.

nodes.name: constructive proof
nodes.statement: In particular, a constructive proof avoids proofs by contradiction and does not invoke the law of excluded middle $\phi\lor \neg \phi$ as a general principle.

nodes.statement: An algebraic closure of $\ring{Q}$ is obtained as the union of an increasing tower of number fields $\ring{Q}(\alpha_i)$, for $i\in\ring{N}$, each an explicitly constructed splitting field over the preceding one.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem
nodes.statement_short: $\bar{\mathbb Q}$ is built as the union of an increasing tower of explicitly constructed splitting fields.

nodes.name: classically
nodes.statement: The wedding of constructive and classical logics is arranged through a predicate $\op{\it classically}~\phi$ that marks every result proved by classical logic. The definition of $\op{\it classically}~\phi$ is \[ \op{classically}~\phi : Prop := \forall {b:\op{\tt bool}}, (\phi\to b) \to b. \]
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: classically as double negation translation
nodes.statement: When $\phi$ is quantifier free, this is essentially the usual double negation translation of a classical formula into constructive logic.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: Use of classically in proofs of boolean goals
nodes.statement: The definition of {\it classically} works in such a way that $\phi$ may be used as an assumption in the proof of any boolean goal $b$, whenever $\op{\it classically}~\phi$ is known.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem
conclusions: $\phi$ may be used as an assumption in the proof of any boolean goal $b$

nodes.name: Function extensionality fails in Coq
nodes.statement: Function extensionality does not hold in Coq; that is, it is not provable that two functions are equal, if they are provably equal on every input.

conclusions: Function extensionality does not hold in Coq

nodes.name: No general decision procedure for mathematics
nodes.statement: There is no general decision procedure for mathematics as a whole.
conclusions: There is no general decision procedure for mathematics as a whole.

nodes.name: first-order formula with equality
nodes.statement: A {\it first-order formula with equality in the predicate calculus} is a formula built from variables $x,y,\ldots$, logical operations $\neg, \land, \Rightarrow,\ldots$, $n$-ary function symbols $f,g\ldots$, $n$-ary predicate symbols $P, Q,\ldots$ and quantified variables $\forall x, \exists y,\ldots$, according to syntactic rules that we will not spell out here.
nodes.definiendum: first-order formula with equality in the predicate calculus
differentia: built from variables $x,y,\ldots$, logical operations $\neg, \land, \Rightarrow,\ldots$, $n$-ary function symbols $f,g\ldots$, $n$-ary predicate symbols $P, Q,\ldots$ and quantified variables $\forall x, \exists y,\ldots$

nodes.name: Example of a first-order formula
nodes.statement: For example, \[ ((\exists x.~P(x)) \Rightarrow (\forall y.~Q(y))) \Leftrightarrow (\forall x\forall y.~P(x)\Rightarrow Q(y)) \] is a first-order formula.

nodes.name: First-order logic forbids quantifying over functions and predicates
nodes.statement: In contrast to higher-order logics discussed earlier, in a first-order formula, quantifiers over function symbols and predicate symbols are not allowed.

nodes.name: refutation complete
nodes.statement: We are interested in algorithms that are {\it refutation complete}; that is, given the input of an unsatisfiable first-order formula, the algorithm outputs a proof of its unsatisfiability.
differentia: given the input of an unsatisfiable first-order formula, the algorithm outputs a proof of its unsatisfiability

nodes.name: Refutation completeness yields proofs of valid formulas
nodes.statement: A refutation complete algorithm can also produce proofs of logically valid formulas, by refuting the negation of the formula.
conclusions: can also produce proofs of logically valid formulas, by refuting the negation of the formula.

nodes.name: Refutation completeness of resolution
nodes.statement: What has been understood for a long time are rules of inference ({\it resolution} together with special inferences that deal with equality) that are refutation complete.
conclusions: rules of inference ({\it resolution} together with special inferences that deal with equality) that are refutation complete

nodes.name: Translation from higher-order to first-order logic
nodes.statement: There are some automated theorem provers based on higher-order logic but the most prevalent practice is to translate problems from higher-order logic into first-order logic, solve them there, then translate the answers back into higher-order logic, with an automated reconstruction of a formal proof inside the proof assistant.\footnote{There are many issues that come up in translating formulas in higher-order logic into first-order logic that I will not discuss here. In particular, some of the procedures might not be logically sound.}
nodes.statement_short: Translate a higher-order problem to first-order logic, solve it with an automated prover, and reconstruct a formal proof in the proof assistant.
output: an automated reconstruction of a formal proof inside the proof assistant

nodes.name: Sledgehammer
nodes.statement: Paulson advocates shipping the goal together with large libraries of theorems to a first-order theorem prover, and letting it figure out which of many theorems to use in the proof~\cite{Paar}. The human is no longer forced to search through the libraries to find the relevant theorems. The method is called a {\it sledgehammer} for its ability to deliver a powerful blow and its complete lack of finesse.
nodes.statement_short: Send the goal with large theorem libraries to a first-order prover, which selects the relevant theorems to use.

nodes.name: Convex hull of three points has measure zero (automated proof)
nodes.statement: Here is one simple example of a theorem proved in this way~\cite{kaliszyk2014learning}. The theorem states that the convex hull of any three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero. The automated procedure was able to comb through large libraries of previously established theorems to locate the following relevant facts: the convex hull is a subset of the affine hull; the affine hull of three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero; and a subset of a set of measure zero has measure zero. The procedure then combines these facts with the necessary logic to give a fully automated formal proof.
nodes.statement_short: Premise selection finds three library facts (hull inclusion, measure-zero affine hull, monotonicity) that prove the convex hull of three points in $\mathbb R^3$ is null.

nodes.name: Convex hull of three points in R^3 has measure zero

conclusions: is a set of measure zero.

nodes.name: Boolean satisfiability (SAT)
nodes.statement: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers implement algorithms that test for the satisfiability of formulas in propositional logic~\cite{marques2009conflict}. Is there an assignment of truth values to propositional variables for which a given formula evaluates to true?

nodes.name: Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)
nodes.statement: SMT ({\it satisfiability modulo theories}) algorithms combine the propositional reasoning of SAT solvers with reasoning within a given theory~\cite{barrett2009satisfiability}. The input to the algorithm is a propositional formula in which the boolean variables have been replaced with predicates from the given first-order theory. An SMT algorithm searches for a valuation of the predicates in the theory that satisfies the propositional formula.
nodes.statement_short: Given a propositional formula whose atoms are predicates of a first-order theory, find a valuation of the predicates satisfying it.

nodes.name: Common constituents of virtual character matrices
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $(\beta_{ij})$ be a matrix of virtual characters, with each entry a linear combination $\pm \chi \pm \chi' \pm \chi''$ of three distinct irreducible characters. Assume the matrix has at least four rows and two columns. Assume the inner product relations \[ \langle \beta_{ij},\beta_{i'j'}\rangle = \delta_{ii'} + \delta_{jj'},\quad \text{for } (i,j)\ne (i',j'), \] with respect to the usual inner product on class functions with an orthonormal basis consisting of irreducible characters. The conclusion is that the virtual characters in each column of the matrix have a common irreducible character as constituent with a common sign.
nodes.statement_short: In a matrix (at least 4x2) of virtual characters, each a signed sum of three irreducibles, with prescribed inner products, each column shares a common signed irreducible constituent.

conclusions: The conclusion is that the virtual characters in each column of the matrix have a common irreducible character as constituent with a common sign.

nodes.name: Proof of the virtual character matrix claim
nodes.statement: A moment's reflection reveals that it is enough to show the conclusion for arbitrary $4\times 2$ submatrices. On each $4\times 2$ block, up to renaming the irreducible characters, a finite enumeration gives all ways to express the entries $\beta_{ij}$ as a signed combination of three irreducibles. Thus, the proof reduces to a case analysis. Symmetry arguments further reduce the number of cases. The case analysis is done by hand in~\cite{peterfalvi2000character}. In the formal proof, Th\'ery programmed the claim into a quantifier-free problem with uninterpreted symbols in an SMT solver. The SMT solution was then transcribed into a formal proof in Coq~\cite{gonthier2013machine}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $4\times 2$ submatrices, then a finite case analysis (cut down by symmetry), done by hand or by an SMT solver whose output is transcribed into Coq.

nodes.name: Reduction of integral-domain polynomial systems to Groebner bases
nodes.statement: If $S$ is any system of equalities and inequalities of polynomials that holds in every integral domain of characteristic zero, then it can be transformed into a Gr\"obner basis problem over $\ring{Q}$.
assumptions: $S$ is any system of equalities and inequalities of polynomials that holds in every integral domain of characteristic zero
conclusions: it can be transformed into a Gr\"obner basis problem over $\ring{Q}$.

nodes.name: Homotopy type theory (HoTT)
nodes.statement: Homotopy type theory (HoTT) is a foundational system for mathematics that includes dependent type theory, the univalence axiom, and higher inductive types.
differentia: includes dependent type theory, the univalence axiom, and higher inductive types

nodes.name: HoTT has set quotients and function extensionality
nodes.statement: HoTT has set quotients and function extensionality, giving remedies to some of Coq's nuisances.
conclusions: HoTT has set quotients and function extensionality

nodes.name: Grayson's classifying space in HoTT
nodes.statement: As an example, we list Grayson's code that constructs the classifying space as the type of a torsor in HoTT~\cite{Ktheory}. We include his proof that the classifying space $BG$ is connected.

nodes.name: Four-Color Theorem
nodes.statement: Variable R : real_model. Theorem four_color : (m : (map R)) (simple_map m) -> (map_colorable (4) m).
conclusions: (map_colorable (4) m).

nodes.name: Prime Number Theorem
nodes.statement: // Prime Number Theorem: ((\n. &(CARD {p | prime p $\land$ p <= n}) / (&n / log(&n))) ---> &1) sequentially
nodes.origin_citation: Hadamard; de la Vallee Poussin; Harrison 2009
conclusions: ((\n. &(CARD {p | prime p $\land$ p <= n}) / (&n / log(&n))) ---> &1) sequentially
nodes.statement_short: The prime counting function is asymptotic to $n/\log n$.

nodes.name: Brouwer fixed point theorem
nodes.statement: $\forall$ f:real$^N$->real$^N$ s. compact s $\land$ convex s $\land$ ~(s = {}) $\land$ f continuous_on s $\land$ IMAGE f s SUBSET s $\Longrightarrow$ $\exists$x. x IN s $\land$ f x = x
assumptions: compact s $\land$ convex s $\land$ ~(s = {}) $\land$ f continuous_on s $\land$ IMAGE f s SUBSET s
conclusions: $\exists$x. x IN s $\land$ f x = x
nodes.statement_short: A continuous self-map of a nonempty compact convex subset of $\mathbb R^N$ has a fixed point.

nodes.name: Central limit theorem
nodes.statement: theorem (in prob_space) central_limit_theorem: fixes X :: "nat $\Rightarrow$ 'a $\Rightarrow$ real" and $\mu$ :: "real measure" and $\sigma$ :: real and S :: "nat $\Rightarrow$ 'a $\Rightarrow$ real" assumes X_indep: "indep_vars ($\lambda$i. borel) X UNIV" and X_integrable: "$\bigwedge$n. integrable M (X n)" and X_mean_0: "$\bigwedge$n. expectation (X n) = 0" and $\sigma$_pos: "$\sigma$ > 0" and X_square_integrable: "$\bigwedge$n. integrable M ($\lambda$x. (X n x)$^2$)" and X_variance: "$\bigwedge$n. variance (X n) = $\sigma^2$" and X_distrib: "$\bigwedge$n. distr M borel (X n) = $\mu$" defines "S n $\equiv$ $\lambda$x. $\Sigma\,$i<n. X i x" shows "weak_conv_m ($\lambda$n. distr M borel ($\lambda$x. S n x / sqrt (n * $\sigma^2$))) (density lborel standard_normal_density)"
nodes.statement_short: Normalized sums of i.i.d. mean-zero random variables with finite variance $\sigma^2>0$ converge weakly to the standard normal.
conclusions: "weak_conv_m ($\lambda$n. distr M borel ($\lambda$x. S n x / sqrt (n * $\sigma^2$))) (density lborel standard_normal_density)"

nodes.name: Kepler conjecture
nodes.statement: The Kepler conjecture asserts that no packing of congruent balls in $\ring{R}^3$ can have density greater than the face-centered cubic packing.
assumptions: no packing of congruent balls in $\ring{R}^3$
conclusions: can have density greater than the face-centered cubic packing.

nodes.name: $\alpha$-equivalence
nodes.statement: In the following rules, we assume that $p$ and $p'$ are equal, up to a renaming of bound variables, and similarly for $b$ and $b'$. (Such terms are called $\alpha$-equivalent.)
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL
differentia: equal, up to a renaming of bound variables

nodes.name: Reflexivity of equality (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: Equality is reflexive: $$ \frac{a}{\vdash a=a} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Transitivity of equality (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: Equality is transitive: $$ \frac{\Gamma \vdash a=b;~~~\Delta\vdash b'=c} {\Gamma\cup\Delta \vdash a=c} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Congruence of application (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: Equal functions applied to equals are equal: $$ \frac{\Gamma\vdash f=g;~~~\Delta\vdash a=b} {\Gamma\cup\Delta\vdash f\hskip0.1em a = g\hskip0.1em b} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Abstraction rule (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: The rule of abstraction holds. Equal function bodies give equal functions: $$ \frac{x;~~~\Gamma\vdash a=b} {\Gamma \vdash \lambda x.\ a~=\lambda x.\ b} ~\hbox{\ (if $x$ is not free in $\Gamma$)} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Beta-reduction rule (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: The application of the function $x\mapsto a$ to $x$ gives $a$: $$ \frac{(\lambda x.~a)\, x} {\vdash (\lambda x.\ a)\, x = a} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Assumption rule (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: Assume $p$, then conclude $p$: $$ \frac{p\hbox{:} bool} {p \vdash p} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Equality-based modus ponens (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: An `equality-based' rule of modus ponens holds: $$ \frac{\Gamma\vdash p;~~~\Delta \vdash p'=q} {\Gamma\cup \Delta \vdash q} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Deduction antisymmetry rule (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: If the assumption $q$ gives conclusion $p$ and the assumption $p$ gives $q$, then they are equivalent: $$ \frac{\Gamma \vdash p;~~~\Delta\vdash q} {(\Gamma\setminus q)\cup (\Delta\setminus p) \vdash p=q} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Type variable substitution (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: Type variable substitution holds. If arbitrary types are substituted in parallel for type variables in a sequent, a theorem results.
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: Term variable substitution (HOL rule)
nodes.statement: Term variable substitution holds. If arbitrary terms are substituted in parallel for term variables in a sequent, a theorem results.
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL
